blocks.x: Okay. Okay. Okay. Okay. Okay.
Okay.

Okay. I have all my notes here. All right. Written on the best, one of the best eating establishments in New Orleans. I wrote my notes out this morning while eating breakfast at the Bluebird Cafe. Where's that?
Right on Pretend. Don't go on Saturday or Sunday.

It's crowded. So we can do it this way. Okay. What's today's date? Today's the August? 13th. 13th of August, 1989. Interview with Al Rose about Louis Armstrong. Okay. I'm just going to roll with it here. Diana. Oh, Diana Rose is here too. Besides Al. Quiet. She's going to be quietly here.
Okay.

I'm learning too. She's learning too. Okay. Great. Here are all my copious notes that I took this morning. You're preparing for this interview. Okay. I'm making sure the microphone is on. Let's see. Yeah, right. Don't worry. Don't worry. We're going to get Al. We're going to get everybody. Anyone who's involved in this is going to get picked up. Don't worry. Now, we were talking, one thing, I want to start off with location of Louis, where Louis was born. Jane Alley. Jane Alley. Jane Alley. Jane Alley. Okay. Yeah. We've had some confusion as to where Jane Alley is. Right. Maybe it's confusion on my part. Well, it's confusion on somebody's part because somebody else said the same thing you did. Exactly. Yeah. My only criteria for that is the fact that I can remember when the tiles were in the alley. Okay. Which said Jane Alley.
And it was in a little street directly opposite City Hall, which goes, it's a parking lot now
that goes from Loyola to the
South Rampart Street. Okay.
So it goes from, it's on which side of Rampart? Where on Rampart? Well, it's towards Loyola. Okay. It runs, what is that, east-west?
Oh, I don't know about that. North-south? Okay.
But it's in the middle of the block, about the middle of the block? In the middle of the block, yeah.
And there's a brick wall there with a tree going through it, which is the, the, the, the tree that he used to climb, that he talked about. The China Ball. China Ball tree. That's still there. Okay.
Well, what's the confusion? Why am I thinking Jane Alley up by Paris Prison?
I don't know. Unless there was a James Alley up there, someplace, but it might be from that. Yeah.
So you don't think Louis, Louis grew up, could he have grown up in both places? I'm just, you know, is it possible?
Well, it's possible.
Yeah. Sure. What's the question?
Oh, well, he's frequently confused. Okay.
Well, that's something we'll get into. Yeah. So it's a possibility he's confused about the location of where he was born.
That he's confused, but I'm not confused. Oh, okay.
All right. All right. Well, we can end the interview now.
Okay.

House not confused. Yeah. All right. So when his, when his, when he was, when he was, when he was, when he was being, I'm running ahead now on the list of my list of questions, but I'm going to probably do that a lot. When his house was being torn down, were you involved with the preservationist movement, you know, to save the house?

Well, there wasn't, there wasn't a real preservationist movement. Well, I heard that the house was going to be torn down by Pete Ricca. So I went to Pete Ricca and said, I would like to buy the house. And he said, you're too late because I already got the contract to tear it down. And he said, I got to go ahead with it. Uh-huh. So I couldn't do it. We didn't even come to money at that time.
Yeah. So he, there wasn't any.
Right. Same thing happened later with mahogany hall.
Oh, okay. But was, was there, I say quote unquote, was anybody else interested in buying besides you? No. Or, or, or, cause I heard there was some other people who were trying to, to do that.
Well, they never mentioned it to me. Oh, okay.

So you didn't know of any, I think Dick Allen had mentioned something about it. I don't know of anybody else. At that time when Louis was, when that house was being torn down. Mm-hmm. What was the, what, do you think the city would have had any sentiment at that time to preserve
it? No. They wouldn't have given a, a damn about it.
But that was the general, that's the general feeling of that.
Yeah. Sure. Because there wasn't any way they could see that you could make any money off it. Mm-hmm. Now they would be able to see it, but then they couldn't.
Well, why did they tear, they tear that area, that down? Why?
Because they had a contract for a parking lot across from city hall.
Okay. What, what year was this?
What year are we talking about? It was, uh, maybe 1950. Mm-hmm. That's close.
Yeah, is that in the ballpark around 1950? Mm-hmm.
Yeah.
Well, but that was during, that was during the Morrison administration. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. Okay. Uh, what, what do we know about, about Louis' mother, basically? What, and. Well, I don't know much about Louis' mother. Yeah. Yeah.
Um, I mean, you know, I never really was involved in researching Louis, it's just I had a lot of personal contact with him.
Yeah, that's, yeah, but, so what, what do you know, I just, uh, of Louis, of Louis' mother?

I don't know, I know that his sister was, uh, always, always wanted to get somebody to bring her veal chops, and, uh. Beatrice? Yeah, and, uh. Beatrice? Yeah, and if you wanted to get an interview with her, you had to bring her veal chops.
Oh, really?
Uh-huh.
Did you interview her? Did you meet her?
I met her, but I didn't actually interview her. Uh-huh. Uh, I went with somebody who was interviewing her, but I can't remember who it was.
Oh, but, but she was interviewing her?
It might have been Rudy Blish. Oh. Pretty, uh, probable. Oh, okay. And, uh, anything else about the family's father?
Uh, no, I didn't know Henry either, but I heard about him, you know, but I never met him.
Doc Sushan knew him.
Uh-huh. Doc knew Louis' father? Uh-huh.
Louis' father at the time. He went to interview him or to find him, you know?
Yeah. Did he, but I think he died in, uh, mid-1930s sometime?
Oh, no, no, he lived a lot longer than that. Uh-huh. He died in the 50s. In the 1950s?
I'm sure. Okay. Okay, um. There's some confusion as to when Louis started playing. Yeah. When, when, when do you think he played? Before, do you think he was playing before he went to the Waves Home?
No, I'm sure he wasn't. First place he didn't have an instrument, and as far as I could tell, he wouldn't have had access to an instrument.
Uh-huh.

Uh, I don't even know if he was that much interested in it. Uh-huh. You know, we just heard some musicians around town like we all did. Yeah. And I assumed that he responded positively to it, but I'm, I'm not, uh, the really great musicians were contemporaries of his, so I doubt whether he'd have been influenced by anybody. Uh-huh. Uh, I'm sure he heard Bolden, but I don't think that he had a clear picture in his mind of who he was. You really, you do think even at his age he would have heard Bolden?
Oh, yeah, sure.
Yeah, sure.

Yeah, right, but I'm, I'm, I'm, I'm thinking, yeah, he may have heard, but he didn't really know. That's right. It was years later that somebody said, oh, you listened to Bolden. Right. That was that person you were hearing.
Exactly. That's the way, that's the way Louie reported many of the things. Yeah. Because people told him later what it was.
What it was, yeah, in time. But that's what I always thought. Uh-huh. He couldn't have been but four or five when Bolden was.
Well, no, Bolden stopped in 1907, so he would have been seven.

Yeah, see that's what I'm saying. He probably didn't have a clear picture as to know exactly, or the name of somebody. Right. Yeah. Uh, yeah, what, how much influence would like his playing in brass bands had on his, on his playing?

Well, he played in the Waif's brass band. Uh-huh. And, uh, he had kind of the responsibility of playing lead horn in that. Uh-huh. And, uh, I'm sure that he felt puffed up about that. Uh, you think so? Yeah. But, uh, he began to attract the attention of a lot of people around here. Uh-huh. And they recognized him particularly. Uh-huh. And then he played in the, in the band with Oliver, the, uh, what was it, Tuxedo, or the Honored, yeah. Yeah. And, uh, got familiar with him there. Uh-huh. But I'm sure that he wasn't, uh, oriented really to being a musician, yet.
How do you, how do you mean?

Well, what I mean is that he didn't consider music to be his life work. He just was, uh, interested in a day-to-day job. Uh-huh. Playing music. I think that it was probably not until he went to Chicago that he began to take music seriously. Oh, you really think so?
That it wasn't until he left New Orleans? I think so, yeah.
Well, he got the job on the boat, you know, but, uh, so that was a job. But I, I don't think he really thought of himself as a career musician. As a musician. Uh-huh.
Until he went to Chicago.
Yeah.
Uh, is it true, is it true that he, that he was not, that when Oliver sent for him, he was not the first considered for the job? Like that?

Well, uh, I would have thought that, uh, that Oliver would have sent for Petit first. Right. See? That would have been the logical thing to do, so, but I don't know that, that he offered the job to anybody else. Right. Because he liked Louis personally. Yeah.
How did, how did, how did those two meet? How did Oliver and Louis?

Well, uh, Louis, uh, went to work in the same band as Oliver. Uh-huh. Uh, I don't know if it was the Honour or the Tuxedo, but it was one of those. Uh-huh. And so they played together in the band and got to hear each other. Uh-huh. And of course, uh, as it turns out, they were both very much impressed. Uh-huh.
With each other. With each other.

Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Of course, uh, uh, neither one of them, would have been directing their attention to appraisals, musical appraisals, because they weren't that sophisticated yet. Uh-huh. And they really, uh, had no idea what was gonna happen down the road. Uh-huh.
Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. What other kind of musical influences would Louis have heard growing up at Liberty and Perdita, or in that area? Uh-huh.

Well, he certainly would have heard whatever marching bands, parade bands were around. Uh-huh. And he would have been, uh, certainly acquainted with, uh, Oscar Celestan. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. And his music. And, uh, and I'm sure that he heard Bunk a lot in Olivier's band. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. And, uh, probably, uh, you know, he would have heard Tony Jackson, for instance.
Would he, would he have heard Tony? Yeah.
He, he certainly should have heard Tony.
Where would, now where would Tony have been played?
Well, uh, Tony was playing in Olivier's band. Uh-huh. He was playing a triangle.
Uh-huh.

Uh-huh. And, uh, but I'm sure that he never followed Tony, you know, like, uh, didn't have any appreciation of his quality until Tony went to Chicago. Uh-huh. But, uh, I'm sure that Petit had some kind of an influence on him.

Oh, yeah. Uh, yeah. Uh, yeah. You know, what, when, when Louis started first working, like, in saloons, like, Matranga and, uh, in that area. Yeah. What, what, what was he playing? What, what, what do you think, what type of music was he playing? Well, he would have been playing the standard, he would have been playing a lot of blues.
Exactly. Yeah. Yeah.
That's what I would think of. Yeah, naturally.

And Louis always seemed to gravitate to the blues, anyway. Yeah. It was the kind of music that he really liked, and, and it, to a certain extent, put him out of step with the rest of the New Orleans musicians. Mm-hmm. Because they didn't play, uh, you know, blues as the main part of their action. Right. Um, but you have to consider what existed at that time musically.
Mm-hmm.
I know that, uh, he played in the Glowman, for instance. Mm-hmm. Which is by Ann Portescue Harrison. Mm-hmm. Of Bayou Road. And, uh, because it was an extremely popular piece around that time.
Mm-hmm.
And, uh, I'm sure he played Tiger Rag, or a version of Tiger Rag.
Yeah.
Uh, didn't have the title yet, but I'm sure he played it.
Yeah, yeah.
And, uh...
There were probably bits and pieces of a lot of melodies floating around.

And Sister Kate. Yeah. Would have been standard in his repertoire. Mm-hmm. Um, he probably also played songs of the Spanish-American War. Mm-hmm. Just before the Battle Mother. Mm-hmm. And, uh, I would be almost sure that he would have played that.
Uh-huh.

Um, I don't know, of course, what his repertoire was. Louie never said what his repertoire was. Of course he wouldn't remember. Mm-hmm. He wouldn't remember what he was playing in those days. Yeah. And most of the things that we think of that he should have been playing, weren't even written
yet.
Uh-huh. So you have to consider that. Yeah.
Well, that's what I'm about getting back to Snatch's melodies. Yeah. Probably floated around and were kind of a common base for... That's right.
For everybody.
For everybody. And then, years later, it was actually published and somebody took writer's credit for it. Yeah.

Certainly, uh, uh, James A. Bland's material had to be in his repertoire. Uh-huh. You know, like, uh... What songs? Oh Them Golden Slippers. Yeah. And, uh, In the Evening by the Moonlight. Mm-hmm. Those things had to be.
Now, was Louie playing, and of course, obviously, I mean, this may be an obvious question, was he playing when he worked in New Orleans? Did he work for both black and white audiences?
Yeah. No, he was... Well, of course, he worked outside a lot, and when he was working on the, on the, uh, you know, in the Marable band, he was playing for exclusively white audiences.
Yeah, I know in Marable, he would have been all white. Yeah. But when he was working in saloons, would that necessarily have all been black?

Well, if he was working over there on Perdido Street, he was working for black audiences. Yeah. If he was working in Red Onion, he'd have been working for mixed audiences. Uh-huh. That was about the only place in town. Yeah. And, uh, if he, he never worked in Pete Lala's or any place like that. Uh, but in, in Segretto's, he was just working with a piano player. Yeah. And, and that was for a white audience.
In Segretto's?
Mm-hmm.
And that was on, that was on Perdido. On Perdido Street, yeah.
That's been replaced by City Hall. Yeah, right.

I know. I can restructure the whole area, right? Yeah. I'll tell you a joke, whether or not, but... Poor House is on Graffier Street. Yeah. And, and the, and the Supreme Court is right with it. Yeah. I think that's got this correct logic, I think, going on. Anyway, uh, I'm probably ahead of myself, yeah. Um, yeah, well, when he worked here in the saloons, were, were, were, I was saying that he played a lot of blues because there was, he was working for a prostitute audience, a lot of it, a lot of it.

Well, they didn't particularly go for the blues. Really? That wasn't their music. Uh-huh. You know, the, the test piece that they used for the piano players in the whorehouses, Yeah. was Poets and Peasant Overture. If you couldn't play that, you didn't get the job. Poets and Peasant Overture?
Yeah.

And, uh, the piano players mainly played classical music. Uh-huh. And, uh, the madams especially didn't care for, for, for, for, ragtime. Jazz, blues, ragtime. Sure. Yeah. And, uh, but blues never somehow filtered into the environment. I mean, they just didn't play the blues here. Uh, the city never produced any significant blues singers. Yeah. People like Lizzie Miles or, or Blue Lou weren't really blues singers, they were pop singers. Uh-huh. And Lizzie got famous for singing obscene lyrics. And, uh, the, uh, the only real blues singer that I knew was New Orleans' Willie Jackson.
Well, why do you think that is, that we didn't produce any blues?

Well, because it's not indigenous. You see, the thing is that the blues, uh, really belong to a different geographical area. Uh-huh. And, uh, this was a stomp town. I mean, you didn't have the kind of moaning and groaning and unhappiness in New Orleans as you had in the country. Uh-huh. And, uh, if you were from Clarksdale, Mississippi or something like that, then you were into the blues. Uh-huh. Another thing that people don't think about is the fact that in other areas of the country where slaves were, came in through other ports, they were all Protestant colonies. Right. And the Protestant colonies didn't even allow secular music at all. So they had to do religious music, which eventually developed gospel music, out of which the blues grew.
Uh-huh.
And the New Orleans music grew as a result of the amalgam of military music and the minstrels.
Uh-huh.
And, uh, and eventually, you know, became a whole different musical form. And they just didn't think in that form. Uh-huh. But most of the historians don't even think about that.

Well, it's most of them from other places. Yeah. Sure. Oh, shall remain nameless. Um, so you don't think, so you don't think when Louie was working those saloons at Liberty Perdido in that area, that he was, that he, that he wasn't playing a lot of blues?
No, he would play an occasional blues, I'm sure. Uh-huh.
But, uh. But the bulk of his repertoire.
Yeah, it would have been stomps.
But up-tempo. Up-tempo dances.
Dances.
Dances.
Yeah. Uh-huh. That's a good thing.
That's a good thing. Yeah. Uh-huh. Oh, yeah, you know about this. In 1909, the, uh, I'm gonna pronounce it wrong, the Gay Shattuck Law? Gay Shattuck Law.
Shattuck Law?
Yeah. What influence, what, what, what effect did that have on saloons at that time? Well, when that amendment was passed?

It put a lot of musicians out of work because it, it caused a lot of the saloons to close. Uh-huh. Since, uh, uh, really that was pressure from the rest of society. Right. You know, wanted to stimulate the cabaret business in other parts of town. Uh-huh. But, uh, uh, the Gay Shattuck Law inhibited the development of music. It wasn't as bad as the close down on the, you know, on Easter Sunday of, of 1913. Uh-huh. But you have to remember that Louie never worked in any of those places.
Where, what, what, what?
In the district. He never worked any place in the district.
Yeah. So, story built. Yeah.
Okay.
Uh-huh.
Although he didn't know that.

No, well, I was just wondering if we were going to get to that. Yeah. Um, yeah, what, what, was that, was that, how, was there, uh, can you see, uh, uh, Dimanche, I mean, uh, some, uh, number, how many saloons closed? I mean, was it X amount closed or, you know?

I would say that at least 10% of the saloons closed. Uh-huh. Because then I had all kinds of little Mickey Mouse things in it, you know? Uh-huh. Like you had to have eight inches off the floor. Uh-huh. To be, uh, to, to be classed as a cabaret. Uh-huh. You had to have a platform eight inches off the floor, all that kind of stuff. And a lot of people just didn't bother with that. Yeah, I'm sure. And a lot of people continued to operate illegally under the, you know, even with the gay shadow court. Right. Nobody wanted to enforce it. Uh-huh. And then nobody did. There was never a conviction in the gay shadow court.
Wasn't there also, uh, the, the, it said that blacks and whites couldn't mingle in the same saloon? Oh, yeah. And was that enforced, or?
Not really, because they did, in fact, in certain saloons.
Yeah.
Certainly in the Red Onion that was always a mixed crowd. And then Pete Lawless was a mixed crowd. Uh-huh.
But that, was that, was that common, uh, in, in, in the number of saloons? I mean, they had mixed, blacks and whites, I mean, was, it was, you didn't, you, you wouldn't

have gotten the idea that they were separated by segregation laws. Uh-huh. But rather by then, their own social tendencies, you know. Uh-huh. And, uh, uh, you wouldn't have felt that people would have, uh, refused to go to a place because it was black or white or whatever.
Uh-huh.
So, you had a certain amount. And not only that, it was always hard to tell in New Orleans anyhow.

Right. Yeah, when somebody's black or white. Sure. Uh-huh. Well, yeah, okay, rolling past the gay Shattuck. Yeah. Well, okay, you brought up 1913, what happened in Storyville. Well, how did that, did that affect?
Oh, that had a big effect, yeah. In 1913, the owners of the tuxedo and the, and of the entertainers, the 101 rank. Right. There was a big shootout there in a tuxedo and they were both killed.
Uh-huh.
And the police came and shut down all the cabarets in the district.
Yeah, okay, in that area. Yeah.

Right. Well, of course, the cabaret business was about shot in the rest of the city because people were going down to the district for entertainment, for the most part. And a lot of the musicians just packed up and left town. The real exodus of musicians started in 1913, not in 1917 when the district was closed. Right. Legally. And so most of them went up north, like Perez and all the people who led bands in the district were gone. How long was the shutdown? Well, the shutdown lasted, I mean, until the district was closed.
Wait, so between 1913 and 1970? Yeah, no cabaret music. There was no, there were no live bands and people?

Well, there were a couple of places that were able to get permits, but the restrictions were so severe included in the permits that they just didn't operate. Yeah. The Tuxedo, for instance, reopened with Celestan, but it was so restrictive that it only, it took Celestan, you know, playing that Mickey Mouse dance music that he could play to satisfy the authorities. Mm-hmm. But the real jazz was all gone. Yeah.

What, um, so, you know, getting back, we had said, did Louie work the district? Did he play? Never. Okay, never did. Never, never. Isn't there, didn't he, um, correct me, I'm just picking this out, didn't he work some gigs with Oliver, or he says he worked? He did, but not in the district.
Oh, okay. He never worked with Oliver in the district.
Um, and he says he worked for Pete Lala at one point, didn't he? Well, that's not true.

He didn't know that it wasn't true, but he never worked for Pete Lala. Oh, okay. See, when I talked with Louie about it, which was right after the big article about him came out in Life magazine. Right. And they had sent me the article first to check out, you know, the, the facts. Yeah. The whole article, as you know, was merely taping Louie.
Yeah, right.

Well, anyway, Louie said a lot of impossible things. Yeah, such as? Well, I mean, he talked about working in the district, for example, which he hadn't done. And, um, he said a lot of things which, uh, which he couldn't have done. In the first place, he wasn't old enough.
Mm-hmm.

But anyway, uh, so I was in Macon, Georgia when his band was there one time, just by coincidence. And I went to see him backstage at the concert hall. Mm-hmm. And I told him, I said, Louie, uh, I hope you don't mind that I made the changes in the article in Life, because it would be embarrassing for you to say a lot of things that didn't happen. Mm-hmm. And he said, yeah, I know. He said, people ask me things that happened 50 years ago. I don't know what happened yesterday. Exactly.
Yeah.

And so he said, I depend on people like you to keep that stuff straight. So I said, well, so I told him some of the things I had changed. And, uh, when we came to the thing about him not having played in Storyville,
Right.
He named all the places that he had played, but none of them were in Storyville. And I told him, I said, none of these places are Storyville. You're in a different part of town.
Which, where?
With Libri Dino. Segretto's and the Trangles.
Yeah, Libri Dino, right.
So, then Tyree Glenn came into the room and Satch told him, he said, he said, Alvin told me that I never played in Storyville. He said, find out that I didn't even know where Storyville was.
Mm-hmm.
So Tyree says, I told you he was ignorant.
Wait, so in Louie's autobiography, when he talks about Storyville.
He's talking about Liberty and Perdita. Yeah.

Yeah. Okay, that's kind of what I gathered. Yeah. I read his autobiography for the 100th time. Mm-hmm. And he's very, he's confused on a lot of things. Oh, yeah. Yeah, a lot of things. Sure. Definitely. I mean, I read the whole thing with a grain of salt. Yeah. That's exciting. Yeah.
Of course, Louie would never deliberately lie about it.

Oh, no. I don't think, yeah. I don't think he'd deliver a lot of anything. I think it was just his memory of, even when he was doing the autobiography, he was, what, 54 years old or 55 or whatever when he wrote it. When it came out, he was, what, 53. Yeah. But I'm sure he wrote it over a number of years. Certainly. And then I'm sure the editor changed things, or probably maybe things that he didn't, yeah, I'm sure. Yeah, of course. Because I've seen some original of the manuscript and it had to be cleaned up. Yeah. So I'm sure there were other changes that probably would have been made before it went to publication. Mm-hmm. So, was there anything, is there anything else that comes to mind on, in that autobiography that was incorrect?

Oh, there were a lot of things, but I don't remember specifically because I haven't read it in years. Yeah. But, what I was thinking of, you know, was that we would talk probably about the, whatever was the extent of my own personal contact with Louis in whatever circumstances. Yeah. And the, see I really didn't know Louis until up north, I never knew him here in New Orleans.
Yes, okay.
And so, the first time I ever met him was in the backstage at the Nixon's Grand Theater in Philadelphia, which is right across the street from Temple University.
Mm-hmm.

And it was a black theater and I used to come out of, out of class and go across the street to the theater all the time, because I knew a lot of the musicians that were, that were playing in the, in the show. And it was during the time when I had first started doing jazz concerts. So it was 1936 and I went backstage, because his band was playing there. And I knew Louis Russell and Red Allen and people that were playing there, Al Nicholas. So, I had, I had met Louis before, I don't actually remember when, but when, when I went backstage, Albert went to introduce me to him. And Louis says, I know this guy, he's the one that Yubi calls Shazam. So, so that, so he identified me with Yubi at that point. And so, I don't remember that we talked about much then, but I, I sat out front and listened to the, to the music. And Baby Dodds and Pops Foster were in the band and I knew them well. They had already worked for me a number of times. So, anyway, that was the first time I met Louis. Second time I met him was about three years later. And that was backstage at the Oriental Theater in Chicago, where the band was playing. And, again, it was the same band then. The next time I saw him in the Oriental Theater was in 1947, I guess. But, when they started the All Stars. Right. Joe Glazer called me. Joe Glazer was a doll. I loved him. But he called me from New York and, at that time, I was running regular Friday concerts in the Academy of Music in Philadelphia. And he said, well, he said, we put together this band of All Stars. And, with Louis Armstrong. And he told me, Jack Teagarden, Barney Begard, and Sidney Catlett. And, the only one I didn't know was Arwell Shaw, who was a kid. And he said, do you want them in Philadelphia? We're going through to the west coast. And I said, well, how much? So, he says, it'll cost you $2,500. Now, I have to tell you that $2,500 in those days. What year were we talking about? What year were we talking about? We were talking about, I guess, 1946. Astronomical numbers. Because those were hard times for musicians. And I was hiring people like Sidney Bechet and Muggsy Spanier, you know, for my regular concerts. And the top price I ever paid anybody was $35. And that was more than anybody else paid. So, it was bad. You get Sidney Bechet for $35. Oh, sure. And anyway, but still, I had a big following in Philadelphia on a mailing list and all that. And I couldn't afford to have Louis go through there on anybody else's auspices. So, I said, okay, I'll take him, John. He says, you won't be sorry. He said, you better take him now because on our way back, when he comes back, it's going to be $4,000. So, I said, okay. So, sure enough, the band shows up and packed the house, upscale prices and everything. And I made a mint on that concert. So, when Louis came back through on his way back, you know, Joe called me, he said, we're on our way back. It's $4,000. I said, it's fine. And from then on, you know, it was kind of upscale for jazz concerts and Louis especially. Mm-hmm. Anyway, Louis came back and I didn't see him very much during the concert time because that's too confused. Yeah. And, but in the meantime, I had gotten a call from Panassier. And Panassier was interested in doing the Nice Festival, which was his first adventure into anything like that. Not that year, but I mean, he was, so anyway. Mm-hmm.
